title: ProactBench: Beyond What The User Asked For
claim: A multi-agent loop with strict information asymmetry between roles prevents leakage and contamination while generating proactive dialogue turns.
layout: 3 columns of agents on top, turn-timeline bands below, dashed arrows, shield threat badges
description: The figure shows three role cards across the top: a purple Planner (tactical orchestrator), an orange User Agent (persona-bound), and a green Assistant Model (response generator). Above each card sits a red shield badge for a threat (T1 style-conf, T2 rubric leak, T3 ext. context). Blue dotted arrows feed each card the inputs it is allowed to see (e.g. persona, scenario, blueprint). Red minus-circle labels on the left of each badge list the information withheld. Below are two gray bands. Band 'Turn t: plan & act' shows the Planner sending a tactical order to the User Agent and writing a rubric box. The User Agent adds orange chat bubbles to a conversation-history box that also holds green assistant bubbles. Band 'Turn t+1: generate response' shows the Assistant Model producing a green bubble from that history only. Color coding by agent carries through the whole figure.
caption: The three-agent loop. The Planner authors strategy and the prospective rubric for turn t+1. The User Agent renders the Planner’s tactical orders as natural messages. The Assistant Model sees only the natural conversation.
abstract: Most LLM benchmarks score how well a model responds to explicit requests. They leave unmeasured a different conversational ability: noticing and acting on needs the user has implied but not said. We call this \emph{conversational proactivity}. ProactBench decomposes it into three phase-tied types: \textsc{Emergent}, inference from a single disclosed anchor; \textsc{Critical}, synthesis across multiple anchors; and \textsc{Recovery}, grounded forward-looking value after task completion. We operationalise the benchmark with three agents: a Planner, a User Agent, and an Assistant Model. Their information asymmetries defend against style-confounded scoring, rubric leakage, external-context contamination, and information dumps. The released corpus contains 198 curated dialogues with 624 trigger points across 24 communication styles drawn from a psychometric inventory and audited by an independent LLM judge. Across 16 frontier and open-weight models, \textsc{Recovery} is both difficult and weakly predicted by six standard benchmarks, making it a useful new evaluation signal.
